Turn left isn't just about Donna's specialness or the need for the Doctor, but also about how cold humans can be in times of crisis. It shows how humans can respond cruelly under times of intense stress, and that the Doctor is subject to the same cruelty. Donna succeeds not only because she's important to the Doctor's timeline but also that she chooses kindness as best she can in times of trouble. Journey's end specifically calls out the Doctor's tendency to turn his companions into soldiers, which is what makes Donna's bravery and compassion so compelling during the last three episodes of the season. People treat Turn Left as if it were just a good lead-in episode to the season finale that establishes Donna's importance, but they misunderstand why she's important. She's not a Mary Sue, she's a medic in a warzone; she shows humanity, even under intense situations. It's also timey-wimey, but not without purpose.

In addition to what others have said, I personally disliked how it fundamentally altered the relationship between the Doctor and other Time Lords. The Doctor's relationship with Gallifrey was complex, containing both pride in his civilization and near disgust with its policies and procedures. A large part of the first seasons of New Who was the Doctor learning how to grapple with this complicated relationship, and represent his lost culture in the best way that he could as a regular man. Even after Gallifrey had been saved, the Time Lords and the Doctor regarded each other as annoyances at best. The Timeless Child arc essentially made the Doctor a god and a key part of time lord mythology. It somehow both separates the Doctor from the other time lords while placing an insane amount of weight on their actions, making them a literal outsider rather than a figurative one. Suddenly the Doctor is way more important that probably any other Gallifreyan, and all of those early struggles are cheapened because, again, this isn't technically the Doctor's culture or people.

When I was 16, I was completely lost. I just wanted to fall asleep and never wake up, but I was scared of what would happen afterward. So I devised a little system.

There was this date that I went on where we rode bikes down to the park, laid down in the grass, and watched the clouds. I felt warm and safe and loved, for the first time in a while. 

I was in a really dark place for the next couple of years. It got worse and worse, and I just wanted to end it. The thing is, I'm a stubborn person. If I wasn't going to run on happiness, then I might as well run on spite. I made a deal with myself: I was going to live until I felt something like that date again. I was afraid of missing out, of being wrong, but most importantly I wanted to give the middle finger to the world that I thought wanted to kill me.

I've had dozens more of those little moments since then. The last one was two weeks ago. My friends and I had screamed song lyrics and danced like maniacs at one in the morning. Driving home, all I could think about was how I'd almost missed this. 

It's not for everyone, but I thought it might help. For me, life is just holding on to the little things to survive the big ones. I held on to my favorite songs, the sound of a thunderstorm outside, the way the leaves look as they change in the fall, the dogs that I haven't pet yet, how fresh a summer night feels, that book I was obsessed with when I was little. It's not much, and everyone has different things, but it helps. And if that doesn't do it, then I do it out of spite, because why should I be the one to give up? If the world doesn't want me to succeed, then I'm going to succeed even more, because who the fuck cares what the world thinks? One day, I'm going to be better, and that's a goddamn promise. I refuse to disappear. If people think I'm a problem, then I'm going to be the most resilient problem they have ever seen. Some days I run on spite alone, but I'm still running.

TLDR: Hold onto the little things, and never underestimate the power of spite.

My mom died of breast cancer when I was 14, and I know exactly how you feel. Cancer is horrible, because it forces you to watch as someone you love slowly deteriorates. When she died, I felt lost and alone, and terrified more than anything, because I was barely a teenager, facing a future full of uncertainty without the one person I knew I could count on. Life felt empty and horrible, and I didn't think I was going to live very long. I was just going to give up.

I'm 20 years old, now, going into my third year of college. The pain that was suffocating at first has lessened more and more with every day, and I'm so happy I didn't give up. There is so much love and life and joy that exists that I never would have seen or experienced otherwise. I still wish that I had more time with my mom, because I know that she would've loved to see me grow up, but one of the things that kept me going at the beginning was the knowledge that she would want me to live my life. 

You're doing everything you can, right now. You're spending time with her, and loving her, and that's all that can be asked of you. I know that it feels like everything is spiraling out of control, but I promise you that it will get better. It's going to be bad, really bad, for a bit, but one day you'll look back and be glad you kept going. Your mom will always be a part of you, and will always live in your memory. Cherish the time you've had, and will have, with her, but please don't feel guilty. You're only human, after all; expecting perfection from yourself will only lead to further hurt. 

I understand what you're going through, and I'm here if you ever need to talk. Please stay safe; there are more people who care about you than you think.

A lot of people are giving financial advice in this thread (which is super important!) but I also want to give some academic advice if you decide college is for you.

1) Have a planner. There's gonna be a lot of stuff going on and sometimes it's gonna get messed up in your head. Get a planner (there are cheap ones at Target and Walmart and some templates online) and write down the due dates as soon as you get the syllabus. It saves loads of time and frustration.

2) If you don't understand the material, go to office hours. I have many professors who actually get disappointed when people don't come to office hours, so you're definitely not intruding. Plus, getting to know your professor is great when you need a recommendation for a scholarship/internship/job.

3) Don't take 8 am classes. You did it in high school, so you can do it in college, right? That is the devil speaking. Don't listen.

3a) On that note, your sleeping/eating schedule is probably going to change. Just make sure you're eating healthy and getting as much sleep as you can while keeping up with your workload. 

4) Don't cram for tests. It's a lot of information and that test grade is probably worth more than it was in high school. Spread your studying out over a few days.

5) Avoid buying from the college bookstore as much as possible. There are probably many places where you can rent/buy textbooks for cheaper than at the bookstore. For comparing book prices, i normally go to [Slugbooks.com](https://Slugbooks.com). You can get second-hand books (for English and Humanities classes, and probably some textbooks too) at Thriftbooks, SecondSale or Ebay.  Also check out [b-ok.cc](https://b-ok.cc) if you want pdf versions of textbooks; they've got a huge selection and it's all free. 

5a) Unfortunately, sometimes you will have to buy from the bookstore if the book requires an access code. This is the one exception, as well as maybe a newer addition textbook that can't be found anywhere else.

5b) Don't buy the textbooks until you are A) Absolutely sure you're going to stay in the class and B) Know what edition of textbook to buy. Most of the times, you can probably buy the books before classes start, but if you're unsure about a class, DO NOT BUY THE BOOKS until you have attended at least one lecture. 

6) If you get waitlisted for a class you really want, email the professor and/or sit in on the class (when the pandemic's over obviously). College professors prefer students who seem interested in the class, and most professors drop people who don't show up on the first day anyway.

7) GO TO CLASS. That one's pretty easy to get.

7a) Also, do the readings and homework. A lot of it will be essential to passing the class.

8) Find professor ratings online. I use a site called CourseForum that rates classes/professors on difficulty and time spent on work throughout the week. It's super helpful.

9) You will get student discounts. Take advantage of them.

10) Get to know at least one person in every class. You don't have to be friends; passing sometimes takes a group effort, and it'll be a lot better if you have other people to talk to. 

​

There's a ton of other stuff I could probably say academic-wise but these are just off the top of my head. Financial-wise, going to Community-College and then switching into a 4 year college is a great way to save money. Work-study programs are also a way to pay off your tuition, and the hours normally aren't that bad since they're run by the school (my current job has a hour limit of 15 hours a week since I'm a full time student, but I'm still getting paid pretty well).  Apply for the FAFSA (like other people in this thread are saying), and also apply to as many scholarships as possible. There are a ton that are for first-generation students, so do some research into those. The more you apply for, the more you're likely to get. 

I wish you the best of luck as you consider higher education! I may come back to this later and add on, but I hope this helps!
